difficultyReason: Two-step causal chain: the weakener must attack the move from 'drug reduced tumor markers' to 'drug will reduce cancer mortality,' not merely one isolated step. One distractor strengthens; one is out-of-scope.
stimulus: Researchers at a prominent oncology institute administered a new compound to patients with early-stage pancreatic cancer. After six months, patients who received the compound showed a 40 percent reduction in tumor-marker levels compared to those who received a placebo. The researchers concluded that widespread adoption of the compound would significantly reduce pancreatic cancer mortality rates.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Tumor-marker levels are not reliably correlated with patient survival outcomes in pancreatic cancer.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The compound produced mild gastrointestinal side effects in approximately 20 percent of trial participants.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pancreatic cancer mortality rates have declined slightly over the past decade due to improved surgical techniques.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Patients who received the compound also adhered more rigorously to dietary recommendations throughout the trial.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The compound reduced tumor-marker levels more effectively in female patients than in male patients.

explanations.correct: The argument moves from 'tumor markers decreased' to 'mortality will decrease.' If tumor-marker levels are not reliably correlated with survival, that bridge collapses — reduced markers need not mean reduced deaths, directly undermining the conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct. Attacks the key inferential link between the measured outcome (tumor markers) and the predicted benefit (mortality reduction).
explanations.B: Out-of-scope trap. Side effects bear on tolerability, not on whether the compound reduces mortality. Does not weaken the conclusion.
explanations.C: Accurate-but-irrelevant trap. Background trends in mortality from other causes do not undermine the claim that this compound would further reduce mortality.
explanations.D: This is a confounder that weakens the premise that the compound caused the marker reduction, but it is a 'too narrow' attack — it questions the causal attribution of the marker change rather than the leap to mortality outcomes.
explanations.E: Irrelevant differential-effect detail. The argument concerns overall mortality reduction; a demographic subgroup difference doesn't weaken that claim.

difficultyReason: Predictive argument from economic data. The weakener must show that the trend cited as evidence will not produce the predicted outcome, not merely that the outcome is undesirable. Includes a strengthener trap and an adjacent-claim attack.
stimulus: Over the past three years, consumer spending on domestic travel has increased by 22 percent while spending on international travel has remained flat. An economic analyst argued that this shift indicates growing consumer preference for domestic destinations and predicted that domestic airlines will post record profits within the next two years.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the analyst's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Domestic airlines have invested heavily in fleet upgrades, substantially increasing their operating costs over the same period.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Consumer surveys confirm that travelers find domestic destinations more appealing than they did five years ago.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several international airlines have begun offering direct routes that previously required connections through domestic hubs.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Spending on domestic lodging has increased proportionally alongside spending on domestic travel.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The increase in domestic travel spending is primarily attributable to higher fuel surcharges passed on to consumers, not to more passengers flying.

explanations.correct: The analyst infers record airline profits from increased consumer spending on domestic travel. If that spending increase reflects higher per-ticket costs (fuel surcharges), not more passengers, airlines are not necessarily carrying more profitable volume — their costs may have risen proportionally, and the revenue increase may simply offset fuel expenses. This breaks the spending-increase-to-profit link.
explanations.A: This weakens the profit conclusion by noting rising costs, which is relevant, but E is more directly targeted: it shows the revenue increase itself does not represent new business, making A a weaker attack by comparison.
explanations.B: Opposite-answer trap. Confirms the preference shift the analyst cited, strengthening the premise rather than weakening the conclusion.
explanations.C: Shift-in-subject trap. Changes to international airline routing affect international travel competition but don't directly undermine the domestic profit prediction.
explanations.D: Out-of-scope. Parallel growth in lodging spending is consistent with the analyst's story; it doesn't undermine the airline-profit conclusion.
explanations.E: Correct. Reveals that the spending metric misrepresents actual demand growth, severing the link between the statistic and the predicted profitability.

difficultyReason: Analogical argument comparing two legal systems. The weakener must identify a disanalogy that undermines the prediction, while distractors attack peripheral details or strengthen the comparison.
stimulus: Legal scholars studying criminal sentencing note that the nation of Valdris reduced recidivism rates by 30 percent after replacing mandatory minimum sentences with individualized rehabilitation programs. Based on this precedent, the scholars argue that adopting similar rehabilitation-focused sentencing in the state of Crestmont would produce a comparable reduction in repeat offenses.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Valdris's rehabilitation programs were designed by corrections experts with decades of experience in criminal psychology.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Crestmont's prison population is composed predominantly of offenders convicted of drug-related crimes, whereas Valdris's was composed predominantly of property-crime offenders, for whom rehabilitation is significantly more effective.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several other nations that implemented rehabilitation-focused sentencing also experienced reductions in recidivism.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Crestmont currently spends less per inmate on correctional services than the national average.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mandatory minimum sentences were originally adopted in Crestmont in response to a spike in violent crime during the 1990s.

explanations.correct: The analogical argument assumes Crestmont resembles Valdris in the relevant respects. Choice B reveals a key disanalogy: the offender populations differ in a way that directly affects whether rehabilitation works — drug offenders respond less well than property offenders. This undermines the analogical inference.
explanations.A: This detail about Valdris's program quality doesn't weaken the argument; if anything, it's neutral or suggests quality matters, but it doesn't show Crestmont can't replicate the result.
explanations.B: Correct. Classic disanalogy weakener targeting the analogical bridge between Valdris and Crestmont.
explanations.C: Opposite-answer trap. Additional confirming cases strengthen the generalization rather than weaken it.
explanations.D: Too narrow / out-of-scope. Lower spending per inmate is weakly relevant at best and does not directly attack the recidivism-reduction claim.
explanations.E: Historical context about why mandatory minimums were adopted is irrelevant to whether replacing them now would reduce recidivism.

difficultyReason: Single-cause causal argument with a well-hidden alternative explanation as the correct answer. One distractor is an opposite answer; one attacks the wrong causal direction.
stimulus: A wildlife biologist reported that in the Fenwick River basin, populations of native trout declined sharply in the three years following the introduction of a non-native crayfish species. She concluded that the crayfish are responsible for the trout decline, most likely by competing for the same invertebrate food sources.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the biologist's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The non-native crayfish and the native trout have been observed feeding in overlapping areas of the river basin.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A viral pathogen lethal to trout was detected in the Fenwick River basin approximately six months before the crayfish were introduced.

choices.label: C
choices.text: In laboratory conditions, trout and non-native crayfish compete directly for invertebrate prey.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Native crayfish populations in the Fenwick River basin have also declined since the non-native species was introduced.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The non-native crayfish species has caused trout declines in two other river systems where it was introduced.

explanations.correct: The biologist assumes crayfish caused the trout decline. If a viral pathogen was already present before the crayfish arrived, the pathogen is a viable alternative explanation for the decline, substantially weakening the causal attribution.
explanations.A: Opposite-answer trap. Overlapping feeding areas support the competition hypothesis, strengthening the conclusion.
explanations.B: Correct. Introduces a prior alternative cause (viral pathogen) that could explain the trout decline independently of the crayfish.
explanations.C: Opposite-answer trap. Lab evidence of direct competition bolsters the biologist's mechanism, strengthening the argument.
explanations.D: Shift-in-subject trap. Native crayfish decline is consistent with the non-native crayfish outcompeting everyone, but it neither supports nor meaningfully undermines the conclusion about trout.
explanations.E: Opposite-answer trap. Parallel outcomes in other river systems strengthen the causal claim about the Fenwick basin.

difficultyReason: Policy argument predicting behavioral change. The weakener reveals that the policy's assumed mechanism won't function as described. Distractors include a narrowly scoped premise-attacker and an irrelevant comparison.
stimulus: A city council member argued that installing speed cameras at the ten most dangerous intersections in the city would substantially reduce traffic fatalities. She cited evidence that cities with comparable camera programs have seen fatality rates fall by up to 25 percent at monitored intersections.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Speed cameras are more effective at deterring speeding than police patrols at the same locations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The majority of fatal accidents at Crestmont's most dangerous intersections are caused not by speeding but by drivers running red lights, a behavior speed cameras do not monitor.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Installing and maintaining speed cameras is considerably less expensive than stationing police officers at intersections.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some cities that implemented speed camera programs later removed them after public opposition campaigns.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Traffic fatalities at intersections without cameras have increased in cities that installed camera programs.

explanations.correct: The argument assumes speed cameras will reduce fatalities by deterring dangerous driving. Choice B shows that the dominant cause of fatalities at these specific intersections is red-light running, not speeding — so speed cameras won't address the actual cause, breaking the mechanism linking the policy to the predicted outcome.
explanations.A: Opposite-answer trap. Showing cameras outperform patrols strengthens the case for cameras.
explanations.B: Correct. Reveals that the assumed mechanism (speed reduction → fewer fatalities) does not apply to the city's actual accident profile.
explanations.C: Out-of-scope. Cost-effectiveness is irrelevant to whether the program will reduce fatalities.
explanations.D: Accurate-but-irrelevant trap. Public opposition affects implementation, not the causal relationship between cameras and fatality rates.
explanations.E: Shift-in-subject trap. A displacement effect at non-camera intersections is a concern but doesn't directly undermine the claim that the cameras will reduce fatalities at the monitored intersections.

difficultyReason: Argument from historical correlation to causal conclusion. The weakener introduces an alternative explanation for the correlation; distractors include a reversed-causation answer and an irrelevant historical detail.
stimulus: Historians examining data from fifteenth-century European cities found that cities with active merchant guilds had, on average, significantly higher literacy rates than cities without such guilds. They concluded that merchant guilds promoted literacy by creating economic incentives for reading and record-keeping.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most calls into question the historians' reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Merchant guilds in some cities also sponsored the construction of churches and public buildings.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cities with higher literacy rates tended to attract more merchants, who then organized into guilds, rather than the guilds developing first.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The cities with the highest literacy rates also had the largest populations in fifteenth-century Europe.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Merchant guilds in different cities varied considerably in their organizational structure and membership requirements.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Literacy rates across Europe increased generally during the fifteenth century regardless of guild activity.

explanations.correct: The historians infer that guilds caused higher literacy. Choice B reverses the causal direction: pre-existing literacy attracted merchants who formed guilds. This alternative explanation — that literacy caused guilds rather than guilds causing literacy — directly undermines the causal conclusion.
explanations.A: Out-of-scope. Guild involvement in construction is irrelevant to the literacy-guild causal claim.
explanations.B: Correct. Classic reversed-causation weakener: the effect (high literacy) preceded and caused the supposed cause (guilds), not the other way around.
explanations.C: Introduces a third variable (population size) but doesn't clearly sever the guild-literacy link; it is weaker than B and more of an alternative explanation for literacy rates generally.
explanations.D: Accurate-but-irrelevant trap. Structural variation among guilds doesn't undermine the correlation or the causal claim derived from it.
explanations.E: This could introduce a common-cause explanation (general literacy trend), but it is vague — it says literacy rose everywhere, which doesn't specifically address why guild cities had higher rates, leaving the historians' correlation intact.

difficultyReason: Technology-domain argument from a sample study to a general conclusion. The weakener attacks the representativeness of the sample; distractors include a strengthener and an attack on a peripheral premise.
stimulus: A software company conducted a six-week pilot study in which employees were permitted to set their own work schedules rather than adhering to fixed office hours. Productivity, measured by tasks completed per week, rose by 18 percent during the pilot. Company executives concluded that abolishing fixed hours company-wide would produce a lasting increase in overall productivity.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the executives' conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Employees who participated in the pilot reported higher job satisfaction than they had before the study began.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The pilot study included only volunteers, who tend to be among the company's most self-motivated employees and are therefore unrepresentative of the workforce as a whole.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The company's productivity measurement system counts tasks completed regardless of the complexity or quality of the work.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Flexible scheduling has been adopted by several other technology firms with positive results.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some departments within the company rely on synchronized team meetings that require employees to be present at specific times.

explanations.correct: The executives generalize from the pilot study to the entire company. Choice B reveals that the pilot sample was self-selected volunteers — the most motivated employees — making the sample unrepresentative. Results from this group cannot reliably predict outcomes for the full workforce, directly undermining the generalization.
explanations.A: Opposite-answer trap. Higher job satisfaction is consistent with and supportive of the productivity conclusion.
explanations.B: Correct. Attacks the generalization by exposing a sampling bias that makes the pilot results unrepresentative.
explanations.C: This weakens the validity of the productivity metric (a premise attacker), but it doesn't directly undermine the conclusion that abolishing fixed hours increases productivity — it questions how productivity is measured, not whether flexible hours cause it to rise.
explanations.D: Opposite-answer trap. Positive results elsewhere strengthen the case for the policy.
explanations.E: This identifies a practical implementation challenge but doesn't directly undermine the causal claim that flexible hours raise productivity; it's a logistical concern rather than a logical defeater.

difficultyReason: Ethical/policy argument predicting a behavioral outcome from a deterrence mechanism. The weakener shows the deterrence mechanism won't operate as expected. Includes a narrowly scoped distractor and a reverse-direction trap.
stimulus: A criminologist argued that publishing the names and photographs of convicted tax evaders in national newspapers would deter future tax evasion. She cited survey data showing that 68 percent of respondents said public shaming would make them less likely to evade taxes.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Tax evasion causes significant harm to public finances and undermines confidence in civic institutions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: People who evade taxes typically do so through complex offshore arrangements that are rarely detected and prosecuted, so few would actually be subject to public naming.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Respondents to surveys about deterrence frequently overstate how much they would be influenced by a given sanction.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Countries that have implemented public-shaming programs for other offenses have sometimes seen increases in those offenses.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The criminologist's survey was conducted among a nationally representative sample of adults.

explanations.correct: The deterrence argument assumes that would-be tax evaders face a realistic threat of being named publicly. Choice B reveals that tax evasion is rarely detected or prosecuted, so few evaders would ever be publicly named. Without a credible threat of exposure, the naming policy cannot deter the behavior, severing the mechanism linking the policy to the predicted outcome.
explanations.A: Out-of-scope. The harm caused by tax evasion is irrelevant to whether public naming would deter it.
explanations.B: Correct. Undermines the deterrence mechanism by showing the threat of public naming is not credible for most potential evaders.
explanations.C: This is also a genuine weakener — it attacks the reliability of the survey evidence — but it is a 'too narrow' attack on the premise rather than the conclusion. Even if survey data overstates deterrence, the naming policy might still have some deterrent effect; B more directly shows the mechanism fails entirely.
explanations.D: Relevant but weak — it concerns other offenses, not tax evasion specifically. The shift-in-subject makes this less directly applicable than B.
explanations.E: Opposite-answer trap. A representative sample strengthens the reliability of the survey evidence.

difficultyReason: Linguistics-domain argument inferring a causal conclusion from co-occurrence data. The weakener introduces a common-cause alternative explanation. One distractor attacks a tangential premise; one is a strengthener.
stimulus: Linguists studying bilingual children found that those who regularly switched between two languages during conversation — a practice known as code-switching — scored significantly higher on standardized tests of executive function than children who spoke only one language. The linguists concluded that the practice of code-switching itself enhances executive function in developing brains.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the linguists' conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Executive function tests are widely regarded as reliable measures of cognitive flexibility and attention control.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Children with stronger innate executive function are better able to manage two languages simultaneously and therefore engage in code-switching more frequently.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bilingual children who code-switch frequently are exposed to a greater variety of vocabulary than monolingual children.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The bilingual children in the study came predominantly from middle-income households with high parental involvement in education.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Previous research has shown that learning a second language, regardless of code-switching, offers some cognitive benefits.

explanations.correct: The linguists attribute better executive function scores to code-switching. Choice D reveals that the bilingual children came predominantly from high-parental-involvement, middle-income households — a confounding variable. Parental educational engagement is a well-established predictor of cognitive outcomes; this alternative explanation means code-switching may not be the cause of the higher scores.
explanations.A: Opposite-answer trap. Validating the reliability of the test strengthens the evidentiary premise rather than weakening the conclusion.
explanations.B: Reversed-causation answer — tempting, but this is actually a strong weakener too. However, D is preferred because it introduces an entirely external confound (socioeconomic/parental factor) that is not entailed by the study's own variables, whereas B attacks only the direction of causation within those variables. Both weaken, but D more directly undermines the study's ability to isolate code-switching as the cause.
explanations.C: Shift-in-subject trap. Vocabulary exposure is a different outcome; it doesn't directly undermine the executive-function conclusion.
explanations.D: Correct. Identifies a confounding third variable — parental involvement and household income — that could independently explain the executive function advantage, weakening the causal attribution to code-switching.
explanations.E: Accurate-but-irrelevant trap. General bilingual benefits don't specifically undermine the claim that code-switching in particular enhances executive function.

difficultyReason: Arts-domain argument predicting an economic outcome from a policy intervention. Weakener reveals that the policy mechanism depends on an assumption that does not hold. Includes one strengthener trap and one out-of-scope distractor.
stimulus: The director of a regional arts council argued that increasing public subsidies for local theater companies would revitalize the downtown arts district and attract new businesses to the area. She pointed to a study showing that cities with robust live-theater scenes have higher concentrations of restaurants, hotels, and retail shops in their downtown cores.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the director's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The study cited by the director controlled for city size and regional economic conditions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In the cities examined by the study, the thriving theater scenes developed after businesses had already established themselves downtown, attracted by favorable commercial rents rather than by cultural amenities.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Local theater companies have reported that increased subsidies would allow them to stage more productions and hire additional staff.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several downtown arts districts in other regions have attracted tourism revenue as well as new businesses.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The regional arts council has successfully administered subsidy programs for visual artists in the past.

explanations.correct: The director's argument assumes that a strong theater scene causes business growth. Choice B reveals reversed causation: in the study cities, businesses came first (drawn by low rents), and the theater scene developed afterward. This means the study's correlation does not support the causal claim that subsidizing theater will attract businesses — the mechanism runs in the opposite direction.
explanations.A: Opposite-answer trap. Methodological controls strengthen the study's reliability, bolstering the director's evidentiary basis.
explanations.B: Correct. Reversed-causation weakener applied appropriately: the supposed cause (theater) actually followed the supposed effect (business concentration), undermining the director's causal inference.
explanations.C: Opposite-answer trap. If subsidies produce more productions and jobs, this supports the overall chain leading to revitalization.
explanations.D: Opposite-answer trap. Examples of other arts districts attracting businesses support the director's prediction.
explanations.E: Out-of-scope. The council's past administrative competence is irrelevant to whether theater subsidies will cause business growth in the downtown district.
